head:
Core · Measurement

Measure to improve: training is not enough

You train, you feel better and better, and nobody ever asks you for a number. This article asks a simple question and follows it all the way through: what is the point of measuring your fitness when you already train? We start from what you feel, move down to what actually happens in the body, then look at what it changes for your health. By the end, you will know what is demonstrated, what is not, and what to do in practice.

The question

Almost everyone thinks a good way to improve is to train more. That is true, and nothing in this article says otherwise. But if that were enough, nobody would need to measure anything: it would be enough to move regularly and wait for the results.

Yet there is a different practice, very common among athletes and in research protocols: you take a standardised test, note the number, compare it with a reference point, then repeat the test later. It takes time, sometimes unpleasant effort, and can give a disappointing result. So it is fair to ask whether it is worth the trouble.

The question

Why training without measuring is not enough: what does a numerical test give you that how you feel and your training do not?

If you have ever told yourself “I can tell I'm improving”, this question concerns you. How you feel is a real tool, but it has never been checked against anything other than itself. As long as it is not compared with a measurement, we do not know whether it is right.

What is at stake

This is not a quarrel between specialists. Five things are at stake for you, concretely.

Your long-term health. The ability of your heart, lungs and muscles to use oxygen (cardiorespiratory fitness) is monitored by cardiologists because it is linked to lifespan. If you do not know where you stand, you do not know whether you are in the zone where improving gains the most.

Your time and energy. Poorly calibrated training, too easy or too hard, costs weeks. Setting an effort requires knowing where you are starting from.

Your independence. Physical capacity declines with age. Knowing how fast yours is changing lets you act before difficulty appears in daily life: climbing stairs, carrying groceries, keeping up with your children or grandchildren.

Your performance. If you are preparing for a race, a competition or a challenge, you need to check that your preparation is having the expected effect, before the big day and not after.

Your mindset. A number can motivate, and it can also discourage. How you receive it matters as much as the number itself, and we will come back to it.

These stakes cannot be left unanswered: each one pushes you to act on a fragile basis, how you feel, as long as it has not been tested. The demonstration that follows goes from the most general to the most precise, in six steps.

  1. Judging yourself by feel: is it reliable?
  2. Why the same training does not give the same result to everyone.
  3. What tracking numbers changes in sticking to a goal.
  4. Is a field test a good instrument, and how do you read a number?
  5. Why this measurement matters for health.
  6. The objections, and what remains uncertain.
rest:
Step 1 of 6We judge ourselves poorly without a reference point

Claim: without a measurement, people place themselves approximately, and usually too high.

Norwegian researchers followed 125 new gym members, all completely untrained at the start. Each rated their fitness from 1 (sitting without moving) to 20 (elite athlete), based on what they could sustain for half an hour. Then their actual aerobic capacity was measured in the laboratory, on a treadmill, with a mask that captures the oxygen consumed.1 On average, participants overestimated their fitness by 17%, or about two notches on the scale.1

On average, we think we are fitter than we are

Index calculated for the illustration: the source gives an average overestimate of 17%, without detailing its calculation. 125 new members of a Norwegian gym. Source: Gjestvang et al., BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine, 2017, based on the ScienceNorway report.1

One could object that this study concerns a particular group. A second, Danish study looks at a broader group: 749 adults aged 30 to 60, who were asked a single question (“is your fitness excellent, very good, good, fair or poor?”) and then compared with a capacity estimated by a cycle ergometer test (the “watt-max”). Agreement between answer and measurement is poor in men (weighted kappa of 0.18) and fair in women (0.27). Kappa is an index where 0 means agreement by pure chance and 1 means perfect agreement: 0.18 is therefore close to chance. On the other hand, the rank correlation is moderate (0.63 in men, 0.67 in women).2

What this means

Your impression ranks people roughly, it does not place them precisely. It tells you approximately whether you are rather fit or rather not, but it can be off by several notches, which matters as soon as you want to choose a training load.

Limitations: the Norwegian author herself considers the scale inaccurate for an individual and thinks that fit people estimate themselves more accurately. The Danish authors conclude that their question is not valid for assessing an individual. Neither study measures the consequences of a wrong estimate: that is a logical deduction, not a result.1,2

Let us accept that how you feel is approximate. Isn't it enough to train regularly to get the same gain, whatever the starting level? That is the next question, and it leads us to look at what happens in the body.

Step 2 of 6The same training does not give everyone the same result

Claim: the response to training varies greatly from one person to another, and it cannot be guessed.

The HERITAGE study had 614 sedentary adults aged 16 to 65 follow the same computer-controlled programme: three sessions a week for 20 weeks, with an intensity set as a percentage of each person's maximal capacity. Everyone therefore follows the same recipe, adapted to their starting level. The result is nonetheless uneven: the group whose power output during training was the lowest relative to that predicted (128 people) gains significantly less aerobic capacity than the one where it was the highest (78 people), even though the average rises in all three groups.3

In finer detail, in 564 of these participants, the researchers tracked seven indicators before and after training: aerobic capacity, fat mass, visceral fat, fasting insulin, HDL cholesterol, small LDL particles and an inflammation marker. Only one person in 564 responds strongly, or weakly, on all seven. And nearly half (49%) combine at least one strong response and at least one weak response.4

Almost nobody responds “strongly” or “weakly” on every indicator at once

564 adults, 20 weeks of endurance training, seven indicators (aerobic capacity, fat mass, visceral fat, fasting insulin, HDL, small LDL particles, GlycA marker). Source: HERITAGE study, abstract published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.4

What this means

Following a recipe that worked for someone else guarantees nothing for you, and an indicator that improves well does not predict the others. You cannot know in advance how your body will react. You can only observe it, by measuring before and after.

Limitations: the participants are sedentary at the start and the programme is cycling endurance, not hybrid training. The abstract does not say why the responses differ.3,4

One clue suggests that measuring also serves to correct. In a 12-week randomised trial, 39 sedentary adults aged 30 to 75, randomly assigned, followed the same training volume (three sessions a week). For one group, intensity was set at a percentage of heart rate reserve, a standard rule. For the other, it was set on each person's ventilatory thresholds, identified from an exercise test with gas analysis. The criterion: a gain in aerobic capacity greater than 4.7%, a threshold that corresponds to the laboratory's measurement error margin. With the standard rule, 12 people out of 20 (60%) exceeded this threshold. With the personalised rule, 19 out of 19 (100%).5

Setting intensity on a personal measurement made everyone improve in this trial

12-week randomised trial, 39 sedentary adults who completed the programme (20 and 19). A responder gains more than 4.7% aerobic capacity, a threshold specific to the study. Source: Weatherwax et al., Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 2019.5

What this means

When effort is set on what your body shows in a test, and not on an average, the probability that your training produces a measurable effect seems higher. This is the central argument in favour of measurement: it serves to set your training, not to grade you.

The limitations are numerous. The sample is small, with dropouts, the researcher knew how the groups were allocated, and the effect concerns aerobic capacity only. The two groups did not have exactly the same absolute intensities: the comparison mixes the method and the intensity level. Above all, the personalisation relied on a laboratory test with gas analysis, not on a field test.5

At this stage: how you feel is approximate, and the response to training is unpredictable. It remains to be seen whether simply tracking numbers changes anything in behaviour, before asking whether field tests are good enough for this use.

Step 3 of 6Tracking your numbers helps you stick to a goal

Claim: in trials, programmes that have people track their own data, with a goal or a reference point, have better results.

Michie and colleagues pooled 122 evaluations of physical activity and healthy eating programmes (44,747 adults). They coded 26 behaviour change techniques and looked for which ones explain the differences in effectiveness. The average effect is 0.31, a standardised “effect size” (the larger it is, the more the programme changes behaviour). Self-monitoring is the technique that explains the largest share of the differences between studies (13%). Programmes that combine it with at least one other control technique, such as setting a goal or comparing yourself with a reference point, reach 0.42, against 0.26 for the others.6

Tracking your data and setting a reference point gives better results

Standardised effect size (axis from 0 to 0.50). Source: Michie et al., Health Psychology, 2009.6

Another meta-analysis converges: 138 randomised trials (19,951 participants) in which an intervention prompted people to monitor progress towards a goal. They clearly increase the frequency of monitoring, and improve goal attainment (effect size of 0.40). The effects are larger when progress is recorded physically (written down, logged) or made visible to others. And it is indeed the increase in monitoring frequency that explains part of the effect on the goal.7

What this means

A test gives the starting point that makes a goal concrete. “Gain a few shuttles in three months” is a goal you can track. “Run better” is not. It is the combination of measurement plus goal that is associated with the best results, not measurement alone.

Limitations: in Michie's analysis, the techniques are not randomly assigned; these are studies compared with one another, with strong heterogeneity (I² of 69%). Above all, this work concerns self-monitoring of behaviours (steps, diet, progress towards a goal), not repeated fitness tests. No source read here shows that a fitness test, taken alone, makes you improve.6,7

If measurement has value, it must be of good quality. Is a field test, taken in a gym or on a track, good enough for that? And a number on its own means nothing: what should it be read against?

Step 4 of 6A field test is a good reference point, with a margin of noise

Claim: a simple test gives a number close to the laboratory measurement, but it moves from one day to the next, and it can only be read relative to your age and sex.

Two qualities are checked separately. The first is validity: does the number resemble the capacity measured in the laboratory? The 20-metre shuttle test (back and forth between two lines, to the pace of increasingly fast beeps) was compared with the laboratory in 57 studies. For the protocol most used in adults (Léger's), the correlation is 0.94 on a scale where 1 would be perfect agreement. It must nevertheless be read with caution: this value rests on a single published correlation for adults, hence a wide confidence interval, from 0.87 to 1.00. The authors speak of moderate to high validity and point out that the score remains an estimate, not a direct measurement.8

The second is reliability: if you repeat the test two days later, do you get the same number? Police trainees (13 people) took the shuttle test twice, 48 hours apart. The group average hardly moved (70.4 then 69.8 shuttles), and the reliability index is 0.92 (0.77 to 0.98), judged excellent. But individually, the difference between the two attempts is 0.55 ± 8.37 shuttles: six people did better on the first attempt (by 8.0 shuttles on average), seven on the second (by 5.9). The authors recommend retesting those who narrowly fail.9

What this means

The test is a solid reference point, with noise. If your score gains three shuttles without any change in conditions, you cannot conclude that you have improved, since a difference of that order occurs from one attempt to the next in people who have changed nothing. That is why the protocol must be followed to the letter, and why we speak of progress when the difference clearly exceeds normal variation.

Limitations: 13 people, a group of trainees, and the source does not specify what exactly the 8.37 represents.9

That leaves how to read the number. Aerobic capacity declines with age and differs by sex. The American FRIEND registry measured 4,494 adults without cardiovascular disease, aged 20 to 79, on a bike with gas analysis.10 At ages 20-29, the median VO2max (the litre of oxygen the body can use per minute, relative to weight, in mL/kg/min) is 41.9 in men and 31.0 in women. At ages 70-79, it falls to 19.5 and 14.8. The authors describe a decline of about 10% per decade.10

The same number does not have the same value at 25 and at 75

MenWomen

Median VO2max (50th percentile). The lines join the two published values, they do not show the intermediate ages. Axis from 0 to 50. Source: Kaminsky et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings, 2017 (FRIEND registry).10

What this means

Between ages 20-29 and 70-79, the median loses a little over half its value in both sexes (calculation from the published values: about 53% in men, 52% in women). An average score at 60 therefore does not mean the same as the same score at 25, and a man and a woman of the same age do not have the same reference point. A norm table by age and sex tells you whether you are ahead of or behind people who resemble you.

Limitations: these medians come from maximal laboratory tests on a bike, with gas analysis, in Americans without cardiovascular disease. They do not apply as they stand to a field test: the norm table for a field test must come from its own protocol.10

We now know that measurement can be of good quality if it is taken rigorously. It remains to find out whether what it measures is worth the effort, that is, whether it matters for anything other than performance.

Step 5 of 6This measurement is linked to lifespan

Claim: the lower the cardiorespiratory fitness, the higher the risk of death, at every level, with the largest gap on leaving the lowest level.

A meta-analysis of 33 studies, pooling 102,980 healthy adults and 6,910 deaths, compares three levels of capacity expressed in METs (one MET is the energy expenditure at rest; a difference of one MET corresponds to running about 0.6 mile per hour faster, or a little under one kilometre per hour). People below 7.9 METs have a risk of death 70% higher than those at 10.9 METs or more, and 40% higher than those at the intermediate level. Each MET gained goes with a 13% lower risk of death.11

The Cleveland Clinic study goes further into detail. It followed 122,007 patients who had taken a treadmill exercise test between 1991 and 2014, classified into five levels according to their age and sex, for 8.4 years on average (13,637 deaths). Between the lowest level and the elite level, the adjusted risk ratio is 5.04: the least fit group has a 5 times higher risk of death. The risk ratios of the lowest level against the higher levels are 1.95, 2.75 and 3.90, which draws a staircase that rises at each level.12

To give an order of magnitude, the same authors quantified in the same study the weight of well-known factors: smoking (1.41), diabetes (1.40), coronary artery disease (1.29), hypertension (1.21).12 The risk of the lowest level against the level just above it (1.95) therefore exceeds that of smoking, and against the elite (5.04) it exceeds it by far. This comparison remains approximate, since it sets a scale side by side with yes-or-no factors. The American Heart Association commentary reports that the statement describes low fitness as a more powerful predictor of mortality than these “traditional” factors.13

A reassuring point for those starting from a low level: the AHA commentary notes that the largest drop in risk lies between the least fit group (less than about 5 METs) and the next one (5 to 7 METs).13 And the lead author of the AHA statement believes that moderate levels of activity in line with the recommendations “may be all that is needed”.14

What this means

Knowing where you stand is health information, not only sports information. It tells you which part of the scale you are on, and therefore where extra effort pays off most. That is why cardiologists ask for it to be measured the way blood pressure is measured.14

That leaves the most serious question: do these links show that fitness protects, or only that healthy people are fit? And what happens when you really improve?

Step 6 of 6The objections, and what remains uncertain

Claim: the links are strong but observed, and no study read here shows that a test, alone, makes you improve.

Reverse causation. A sick person, sometimes without knowing it, performs less well in exercise. Illness can therefore explain both the poor score and the death. The Cleveland Clinic authors themselves write that the association does not prove causation and that it is not known whether high fitness selects patients with low mortality or genuinely reduces mortality. They also point to possible unmeasured factors (social background, origin) and a population of patients referred to a single centre, not the general population.12 In the 2009 meta-analysis, the authors themselves call for a clinical trial to check whether improving fitness reduces risk.11

And if you improve? The study closest to an answer followed 9,777 men from a preventive clinic at two examinations, separated by 4.9 years on average, then for 5.1 years (223 deaths). Men who stayed unfit at both examinations have an age-adjusted death rate of 122.0 per 10,000 per year. Those who went from unfit to fit: 67.7. Those who stayed fit: 39.6. The risk is 44% lower (interval from 25 to 59%) in those who improved.15

Those who improved die less than those who stayed unfit

9,777 men from a preventive clinic, 223 deaths. Source: Blair et al., JAMA, 1995 (article abstract).15

What this means

The group that improved ends up on the side of those who were already fit, which argues for a benefit of the improvement itself, not only of good initial health. But this is not proof: the men who improved may have changed other habits, and no randomised trial read here has measured mortality as a function of a gain in capacity.15

Should you aim for the elite? Not necessarily. The advantage of the elite level over the level just below is 0.77 overall (interval from 0.63 to 0.95), but it is not significant separately in men (0.81) or in women (0.65), and only in the over-70s and the hypertensive among the subgroups.12

A result can discourage. In a quasi-experimental study of 430 students, the group that took an assessment with feedback on the results subsequently shows less intrinsic motivation and sense of competence than two control groups. Among those who judge their feedback negative, physical activity also drops.16 The groups were not randomly allocated, the population is students, the split according to perceived feedback was made after the fact, and the abstract does not detail the content of the feedback. We cannot conclude that every test discourages, but we cannot claim that every test motivates.

What this means

All this points to a way of receiving a result: as a starting point, not as a verdict. Measurement is useful if you have decided in advance what you will do with it.

The answer to the question

The question was: what does a numerical test give you that how you feel and your training do not? Here is the answer, with its level of certainty.

What is solid. How you feel is off: by 17% upwards on average in one study, and unreliable for placing an individual in another.1,2 The response to training varies greatly from one person to another and cannot be guessed.3,4 In trials, programmes that combine tracking of your data with a goal have better results.6,7 And cardiorespiratory fitness is linked to lifespan, at every level.11,12

What is probable. Setting training on a personal measurement improves the chances of progress: a randomised trial points that way, but it is small and uses a laboratory test.5 Improving is linked to a lower risk of death, with the uncertainty of an observational study.15

What is not demonstrated. That a field fitness test, taken alone, makes you improve. That the health benefit of a fitness gain has been verified by a trial. And the ideal interval between two tests.

So, to answer the question: training remains what makes you improve, and measurement does not replace it. What it adds is knowing where you start from, being able to set a real goal, checking that what you do has an effect in your case, and placing yourself relative to people your age. Without it, you train blind, which does not matter as long as it works, but you cannot know whether it works.

What you can put in place

These actions follow from the demonstration. They are ordered, from the first to the one that repeats.

  1. Take the test by the rules.Same protocol, same conditions. Otherwise the number cannot be compared with anything, neither a norm table nor yourself, and the noise of the test (step 4) takes over.
  2. Place yourself on the norm table for your age and sex.The raw number does not tell you whether your level is good. If your result is low, that is where the potential gain is greatest (step 5), not a sign that you should give up.
  3. Write down a numerical goal and a date.This is the combination of measurement plus goal that the most effective programmes have in common (step 3). Also note the conditions of the test: time of day, fatigue, sleep.
  4. Retest in the same conditions and read the difference with caution.Speak of progress when the difference clearly exceeds day-to-day variation (step 4). The studies that measured a gain did so after 12 to 20 weeks of training:3,5 a new test at that order of magnitude is a reasonable practical choice, not an established result.
  5. Compare yourself with yourself.Since the response to training varies from one person to another (step 2), someone else's progress tells you nothing about yours. If your test does not move after several weeks, that is information used to change the training, not to discourage you.

The THW test on this page gives you a number and a point of comparison for steps 1 to 4. It does not replace medical advice: a very low score, chest pain or abnormal breathlessness justify seeking it before training harder.

What these figures do not say
  • No source read shows that a fitness test, taken alone, makes you improve. The results on tracking concern behaviours.6,7
  • The 17% gap comes from a press report, on new gym members, with no calculation detail.1
  • The personalised intensity trial includes 39 people and uses a laboratory test.5
  • The shuttle test estimates aerobic capacity, it does not measure it directly. The correlation of 0.94 rests on a single value in adults, and the test-retest on 13 people.8,9
  • The links between low fitness and mortality are observed, not demonstrated by a trial.11,12

Frequently asked questions

If I feel fit, is a test useful?

Your impression may be right, especially if you train a lot, according to the author of the Norwegian study. The test lets you check it and keep a starting point for what follows.1

Is a field test as good as a laboratory test?

No, it is an estimate. It is highly correlated with the laboratory in adults, but remains a substitute.8

Is a poor result final?

Nothing in these studies suggests so. In HERITAGE, average capacity rises in all groups after 20 weeks, including the one whose power output is the lowest.3 A result is a snapshot of the day.

Is testing more often better?

It is not established for fitness tests. The noise from one attempt to the next limits the value of very close tests.9
